chunks: "Both have the same fundamental and the same low harmonics. What changes is the high end.
A sharp square wave has odd harmonics falling as one over n, so 20 decibels per decade, and that continues out to very high frequency.

A wave with finite, slower edges follows the same line up to a knee frequency of roughly one over pi times the rise time, then falls at 40 decibels per decade, because the edge multiplies the spectrum by a sinc of the rise time.
In numbers, take a 100 megahertz clock.

With a 100 picoseconds edge the knee is about 3 gigahertz; with a 1 nanoseconds edge it's about 300 megahertz, and at 2 gigahertz the slower edge's harmonic is roughly 15 decibels lower (approaching 20 decibels further up, once both are past their knees).
Slowing the edge ten times cuts high-frequency content by ten times, 20 decibels, with almost no effect on the first few harmonics.
If the edge takes up half the period, the wave becomes a triangle and the harmonics go as one over n squared right from the start.
The trade-off is that a slower edge has less timing margin and is more affected by noise at the threshold.
And if the edge is slowed by a real filter, the shape is smoother with no overshoot, which is also visible as the absence of Gibbs-type ringing."
